L8: # Learning Hidden Quantum Markov Models
L9: 
L10: Siddarth Srinivasan, Geoff Gordon, Byron Boots
L11: 
L12: Proceedings of the Twenty-First International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics, PMLR 84:1979-1987, 2018.
L13: #### Abstract
L14: Hidden Quantum Markov Models (HQMMs) can be thought of as quantum probabilistic graphical models that can model sequential data. We extend previous work on HQMMs with three contributions: (1) we show how classical hidden Markov models (HMMs) can be simulated on a quantum circuit, (2) we reformulate HQMMs by relaxing the constraints for modeling HMMs on quantum circuits, and (3) we present a learning algorithm to estimate the parameters of an HQMM from data.
L15: While our algorithm requires further optimization to handle larger datasets, we are able to evaluate our algorithm using several synthetic datasets generated by valid HQMMs. We show that our algorithm learns HQMMs with the same number of hidden states and predictive accuracy as the HQMMs that generated the data, while HMMs learned with the Baum-Welch algorithm require more states to match the predictive accuracy.

L1@P0: Siddarth Srinivasan Geoff Gordon Byron Boots
L2@P0: Georgia Institute of Technology Carnegie Mellon University Georgia Institute of Technology
L3@P0: Abstract
L4@P0: Hidden Quantum Markov Models (HQMMs)
L5@P0: can be thought of as quantum probabilistic
L6@P0: graphical models that can model sequential
L7@P0: data. We extend previous work on HQMMs
L8@P0: with three contributions: (1) we show how
L9@P0: classical hidden Markov models (HMMs) can
L10@P0: be simulated on a quantum circuit, (2) we reformulate HQMMs by relaxing the constraints
L11@P0: for modeling HMMs on quantum circuits, and
L12@P0: (3) we present a learning algorithm to estimate the parameters of an HQMM from data.
L13@P0: While our algorithm requires further optimization to handle larger datasets, we are able to
L14@P0: evaluate our algorithm using several synthetic
L15@P0: datasets generated by valid HQMMs. We
L16@P0: show that our algorithm learns HQMMs with
L17@P0: the same number of hidden states and predictive accuracy as the HQMMs that generated
L18@P0: the data, while HMMs learned with the BaumWelch algorithm require more states to match
L19@P0: the predictive accuracy.
L20@P0: 1 INTRODUCTION
L21@P0: We extend previous work on Hidden Quantum Markov
L22@P0: Models (HQMMs), and propose a novel approach to
L23@P0: learning these models from data. HQMMs can be
L24@P0: thought of as a new, expressive class of graphical models that have adopted the mathematical formalism for
L25@P0: reasoning about uncertainty from quantum mechanics.
L26@P0: We stress that while HQMMs could naturally be implemented on quantum computers, we do not need such
L27@P0: a machine for these models to be of value. Instead,
L28@P0: HQMMs can be viewed as novel models inspired by
L29@P0: quantum mechanics that can be run on classical computers. In considering these models, we are interested
L30@P0: in answering three questions: (1) how can we construct
L31@P0: Proceedings of the 21st International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics (AISTATS) 2018, Lanzarote,
L32@P0: Spain. PMLR: Volume 84. Copyright 2018 by the author(s).
L33@P0: quantum circuits to simulate classical Hidden Markov
L34@P0: Models (HMMs); (2) what happens if we take full advantage of this quantum circuit instead of enforcing the
L35@P0: classical probabilistic constraints; and (3) how do we
L36@P0: learn the parameters for quantum models from data?
L37@P0: The paper is structured as follows: first we describe
L38@P0: related work and provide background on quantum information theory as it relates to our work. Next, we
L39@P0: describe the hidden quantum Markov model and compare our approach to previous work in detail, and give
L40@P0: a scheme for writing any hidden Markov model as an
L41@P0: HQMM. Finally, our main contribution is the introduction of a maximum-likelihood-based unsupervised
L42@P0: learning algorithm that can estimate the parameters
L43@P0: of an HQMM from data. Our implementation is slow
L44@P0: to train HQMMs on large datasets, and will require
L45@P0: further optimization. Instead, we evaluate our learning algorithm for HQMMs on several simple synthetic
L46@P0: datasets by learning a quantum model from data and
L47@P0: filtering and predicting with the learned model. We
L48@P0: also compare our model and learning algorithm to maximum likelihood for learning hidden Markov models
L49@P0: and show that the more expressive HQMM can match
L50@P0: HMMs’ predictive capability with fewer hidden states
L51@P0: on data generated by HQMMs.
L52@P0: 2 BACKGROUND
L53@P0: 2.1 Related Work
L54@P0: Hidden Quantum Markov Models were introduced by
L55@P0: Monras et al. [2010], who discussed their relationship to
L56@P0: classical HMMs, and parameterized these HQMMs using a set of Kraus operators. Clark et al. [2015] further
L57@P0: investigated HQMMs, and showed that they could be
L58@P0: viewed as open quantum systems with instantaneous
L59@P0: feedback. We arrive at the same Kraus operator representation by building a quantum circuit to simulate a
L60@P0: classical HMM and then relaxing some constraints.
L61@P0: Our work can be viewed as extending previous work
L62@P0: by Zhao and Jaeger [2010] on Norm-observable operator models (NOOM) and Jaeger [2000] on observableoperator models (OOM). We show that HQMMs can
L63@P0: be viewed as complex-valued extensions of NOOMs,
L64@P0-1: formulated in the language of quantum mechanics. WeLearning Hidden Quantum Markov Models
L65@P1: use this connection to adapt the learning algorithm
L66@P1: for NOOMs in Zhao and Jaeger [2007] into the first
L67@P1: known learning algorithm for HQMMs, and demonstrate that the theoretical advantages of HQMMs also
L68@P1: hold in practice.
L69@P1: Schuld et al. [2015a] and Biamonte et al. [2016] provide
L70@P1: general overviews of quantum machine learning, and
L71@P1: describe relevant work on HQMMs. They suggest that
L72@P1: developing algorithms that can learn HQMMs from
L73@P1: data is an important open problem. We provide just
L74@P1: such a learning algorithm in Section 4.
L75@P1: Other work at the intersection of machine learning and
L76@P1: quantum mechanics includes Wiebe et al. [2016] on
L77@P1: quantum perceptron models and learning algorithms.
L78@P1: Schuld et al. [2015b] discuss simulating a perceptron
L79@P1: on a quantum computer.
